# Presentation HTML patterns

Reference library for single-file HTML decks. Use this as a menu: not every deck uses every pattern, and no deck should use them all. One idea per slide still rules.

The first half is the pattern library. The second half, Craft depth, is the tactical craft that separates an HTML deck from a world-class one: typography discipline, fixed-stage math, an easing library, contrast rules for full-bleed, SVG generative geometry, presenter view and a steal-list.

## The stage: two canvases, one file

A deck is opened on a laptop in landscape, on a phone in portrait and inside a viewer that plays it in a frame that follows the screen. A single landscape stage scaled to a narrow phone shows small text at a few pixels and letterboxes in a black frame. So every deck has two fixed canvases, picked by frame shape. Same slides, same words, same order; only the layout changes.

**Design for frames, not devices.** The deck gets the frame's width and height as innerWidth and innerHeight, so the canvas choice is made from the frame, never from the device.

- **Landscape 1920 by 1080** when innerWidth divided by innerHeight is at least 1.
- **Portrait 720 by 1280** when that ratio is below 1. One column, stacked: label or chip, headline, key visual or number, supporting text. Never two columns. Low-density slides stay a headline over a visual; stack and enlarge, do not add copy.
- Author in pixels against the active canvas. Use flex or grid, never fixed positions that only make sense at 1920 wide. The switch is the fit() below.
- **Page background equals slide background.** Set html and body to the same background variable the slides use, so any rounding gap or side bar around the stage is invisible.
- **Safe margins:** landscape 96 pixels outer padding by default; portrait 56 by 48 pixels plus bottom padding for the phone home bar. Full-bleed visuals ignore margins; text never touches the edge.
- **Type scale, landscape:** display 128 to 200 pixels, headline 72 to 96, subhead 40 to 56, body 28 to 36, caption 20 to 24. Low-density decks live at the top of the range; pitch and proposal decks at the bottom. Nothing under 20 pixels authored.
- **Type scale, portrait (the 720 canvas shows at about 55 percent on a phone):** body 32 pixels or more, titles 56 or more, big numbers 160 or more, nothing under 24.
- **One section class slide per slide, top level, in order, with stable ids (s1, s2, ...).** A deck over 8 slides shows as a card count in some viewers, so put the strongest slides first. Give every slide a heading.
- Use a viewport meta tag with viewport-fit=cover. Use innerHeight or 100dvh, never 100vh.
- **Phone navigation:** swipe left and right plus visible tap zones on the left and right 20 percent (at least 44 pixels). No hover-only or key-only controls.
- **Deck controls stay visible.** A deck keeps its own previous, next and counter. They are needed on the file page and in a mobile app, and a deck cannot tell reliably that it is embedded. Do not hide the deck's controls.
- SVG visuals get a viewBox and width 100 percent so they reflow into every canvas; a diagram that needs more than 4 labels in portrait is redrawn, not shrunk.

## Self-contained rules (non-negotiable)

The HTML must open offline from a local file with nothing broken, and it must render in a locked-down viewer that blocks every outside script, stylesheet, font and image. Run the viewer-safe-html check before you upload.

- **Size:** a deck is under 150 KB.
- **Inline all CSS** in a style block in the head. No external stylesheets, no font links, no CDN script tags.
- **Fonts:** never embed a font and never write a font-face rule. The viewer blocks all font files, even inlined ones, and a base64 font adds about 130 KB per face. Use the system stack and design every slide so it holds on that stack. If a brand font matters, say in your message that the viewer shows the system font.
- **Images:** prefer inline SVG. Raster images go in as base64 data URLs. Never link to a hosted image the deck might outlive.
- **JS is optional.** Keyboard nav, swipe and counter are about 60 lines. Skip frameworks entirely. Wrap any local storage use in try/catch; the viewer throws on it.
- No analytics, no trackers, no fingerprinting scripts. Ever.

## Agent-readable contract

People and reviewing agents read decks as text, so the markup must be readable without rendering it:

- A title first in the head, then a description meta with a two-sentence summary of the deck, then the CSS.
- One section per slide, ids s1, s2, ... stable across versions, with the speaker notes kept in data-notes.
- Exactly one h1 or h2 per slide, as the slide's claim.
- Lists are real ul and li, tables are real table, not divs in a grid.
- No text in CSS content. No inline style attributes where a class works.
- No font-face, no base64 fonts. A whole deck stays under 150 KB.

## Keyboard nav and counter (baseline JS)

Standard behaviours every deck ships with:

- Right arrow, Space or PageDown goes to the next slide.
- Left arrow or PageUp goes to the previous slide.
- Home and End go to the first and last slide.
- F toggles fullscreen.
- N toggles the speaker notes overlay.
- A slide counter in a corner, toggleable with a period to hide it for demo mode.
- Swipe and tap zones on touch.

Speaker notes go in data-notes on each section and render in a fixed overlay panel when N is pressed.

## Slide patterns (the library)

Each pattern is a compositional template. Pick one per slide, do not stack them. Names are the vocabulary; use them in the outline. Each pattern needs a portrait layout too: columns stack, comparisons go top and bottom, timelines go vertical.

- **Hero:** full-bleed background (SVG geometry or image), single headline over it, optional subhead. Opener, section starts, closer. Pick left-aligned or centred and stick with it across the deck.
- **Section divider:** brand colour field, oversized section number and title, no body copy. Signals a chapter break.
- **Statement:** one sentence, oversized (150 pixels or more), centred on generous whitespace. Use sparingly.
- **Quote pull:** pull quote in editorial hierarchy, attribution in caption size beneath. Never more than 25 words.
- **Data callout:** one big number (200 pixels or more), one-line caption underneath, optional source citation. If you have three numbers, use three-column instead.
- **Three-column:** three parallel items (metrics, features, phases). Equal weight, identical structure per column. Never four; split across two slides instead. Portrait: three stacked rows.
- **Comparison:** two-column, left against right, with a clear axis of comparison. Label the axis in a caption above. Portrait: top against bottom.
- **Timeline:** horizontal or vertical, milestones as nodes, dates as captions. Keep to 3 to 6 nodes; more than 6 means group into phases. Portrait: vertical.
- **Image and caption:** full-bleed or half-bleed image, caption in a corner. The caption carries the meaning; the image supports it.
- **Diagram:** inline SVG for arrows, nodes and flow. Author by hand or generate from a spec, never a screenshot of a whiteboard.
- **List with icons:** 3 to 5 items (4 at most in portrait), one icon per item, one line each. Icons must be a consistent set. If they decorate rather than clarify, drop them.
- **Code or product-native:** mono type, tinted background, syntax colours from the brand palette. Meaningful snippet only.
- **Call to action:** hero-like composition, one clear next step. Never more than one ask.

## Motion patterns

Motion earns its place or it does not ship.

- **Advance-triggered only.** Motion fires when the slide enters view or when the presenter presses next. Never autoplay looping animation behind text.
- **Duration:** 300 to 600 ms for reveals, 800 to 1200 ms for backgrounds.
- **Easing:** default to cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1) for reveals.
- **Common patterns:** fade and rise (opacity 0 to 1 with a 16 pixel translate), numeric count-up, progressive diagram reveal, and very slow ambient background drift on hero or section slides only.
- **Always ship a prefers-reduced-motion block.** Not optional.
- Never parallax scrolling, bounce or elastic easing on primary motion, particle effects, floating orbs or kinetic typography flexes.

## Backgrounds

- **Author SVG geometry** for anything abstract: brand-native shapes, brand palette, sharp edges over gradient blobs.
- **Product screenshots** get a subtle brand-colour frame and a mild drop shadow.
- **Photos** only when the subject matters (a speaker, an event, an actual customer). Grade to the brand palette so they do not feel foreign. Full-bleed photos with text overlaid must pass the contrast rules below.
- **Banned:** gradient mesh blobs, grey noise fills, 3D-generated shapes, generic particle grids, filler droplets. These are the AI-slop tells named in the ban list below.

## Density and dial

Match the slide pattern to the density dial called in the brief:

- **Low-density, speaker-led:** heavy use of hero, statement, section divider, data callout, quote pull and image with caption. Body copy is rare. Speaker notes carry the substance.
- **High-density, reading-first:** three-column, comparison, timeline, list with icons, diagram and code. Written claims are expected on the slide itself.

If you are using more than 2 dense patterns in a low-density deck, or more than 2 hero or statement slides in a pitch, the dial call was probably wrong. Flag it, do not push through.

---

## Craft depth (world-class layer)

The patterns above cover the what. This section covers the how well: the tactical craft that separates production-grade decks from templates.

### Typography

- **One family used systemically.** No second display face; one family, used at scale.
- **No font files.** Do not ship font-face or base64 fonts; the stack is the system stack. Build hierarchy with size, weight and spacing.
- **Turn on font-optical-sizing: auto** at the root so optical sizing tracks computed size.
- **No preload or CDN font links.** The viewer blocks them.
- **Kerning matters more at display sizes.** Enable font-feature-settings kerning where the stack supports it.

### Fixed-stage scaling (spelled out)

- Author every element in pixels against the active canvas: 1920 by 1080 landscape or 720 by 1280 portrait.
- Wrap the whole stage in a container and size it from the active canvas:

```js
function fit(){
  var portrait = innerWidth / innerHeight < 1;
  var W = portrait ? 720 : 1920;
  var H = portrait ? 1280 : 1080;
  stage.style.width = W + 'px';
  stage.style.height = H + 'px';
  document.documentElement.classList.toggle('portrait', portrait);
  var s = Math.min(innerWidth / W, innerHeight / H);
  stage.style.transform = 'translate(' + ((innerWidth - W*s)/2) + 'px,' + ((innerHeight - H*s)/2) + 'px) scale(' + s + ')';
}
addEventListener('resize', fit); fit();
```

- Write portrait overrides as .portrait rules in the same stylesheet. Most slides need none; add one only where a check shows overflow.
- Set html and body background to the slide background variable so the area around the stage matches the slides.
- **Never use clamp(), vw or vh inside the stage.** Reflow inside the stage is what causes the overflow bugs the visual check exists to catch.
- For print or PDF, use a print media rule that bypasses the transform and lays each slide at landscape design size with a page break after it.
- **Baseline grid:** pick a rhythm (8 pixels is standard) and set line-heights that snap to it. Break the grid deliberately, once, for a memorable moment.
- **Check every frame the viewer can make.** Look at every slide at 1920 by 1080, at 1510 by 850, at 856 by 482, at 599 by 337 and at 390 by 844. Pass marks: no overflow, overlap or bottom clipping; the smallest text on screen at least 12 pixels at 856 by 482, at least 9 pixels at 599 by 337 and at least 13 pixels at 390 wide; no side bars; swipe and tap change slides. Measure the smallest text from computed font size times the stage scale, do not eyeball it. Attach a slide grid with landscape and portrait rows and say which viewports you checked.

### Motion: a curve library, not one curve

- cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1) for professional business decks.
- cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1) for premium, calm or editorial registers.
- cubic-bezier(0.5, 1.15, 0.4, 1) for playful registers only.
- **Never linear.** It reads mechanical.

Entrances ease out (fast start, gentle landing), 250 to 400 ms. Exits ease in (get out of the way), 150 to 250 ms. Never symmetric. Micro-interactions 200 ms or less; full slide transitions 600 ms or less.

Always ship a reduced-motion block:

```css
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
  }
}
```

### Full-bleed images: contrast discipline

Text needs 4.5 to 1 contrast against its background (3 to 1 for large text). Over an image, the ratio must hold at the lightest and darkest pixels behind each glyph.

- **Scrim:** a dark overlay, or a gradient scrim biased toward the text edge.
- **Duotone:** an SVG colour matrix or a CSS filter chain to lock the palette to brand hues.
- **Compose the photo for the type:** place headlines in the darkest quadrant deliberately.
- **Text shadow is a last-resort hack.** Use it only when scrim and composition have failed.

### SVG craft: generative geometry that reads brand-native

Inline SVG so you can animate paths, use masks and clip paths, and drive fills from CSS variables.

- **Voronoi cells:** cellular, organic-technical.
- **Phyllotaxis point clouds:** Fibonacci spiral, sunflower-seed packing.
- **Noise fields:** turbulence and displacement for organic textures, behind text only when the contrast rules hold.
- **Flow lines** from a parametric field: directional without arrows.

Rules: keep any single background SVG under 15 KB inline; strip editor metadata before inlining; drive fills from CSS variables so brand palette changes cascade.

### Data visualization: inline SVG over a library for small charts

- **3 series or fewer:** hand-rolled inline SVG, with annotations directly on the mark.
- **More than 3 series:** a real chart library, but strip default legends, gridlines and margins to the minimum.
- **Annotate on the chart,** in the space a legend would waste.
- Prefer small multiples over stacked series wherever the comparison fits.

### Presenter view

The N-key overlay is the baseline. A better version shows the current slide, the next slide, the notes, an elapsed timer and the slide count. Store notes in data-notes on each section. For dual-screen, open a second window with a presenter flag and keep the two in sync.

### Reference stacks: what to steal, what to leave

- **Reveal.js.** Steal: fragment reveal API, Auto-Animate, print-to-PDF export, speaker view. Leave: the default theme.
- **Slidev.** Steal: animated code highlighting and magic-move transitions. Leave: the runtime if the deliverable is single-file HTML.
- **Spectacle.** Steal: sensible typographic defaults. Leave: the React runtime for a one-file deliverable.
- **Impress.js.** Steal: 2D or 3D CSS-transform positioning for one deliberate moment. Leave: it as a default framework.
- **Stripe, Linear, Vercel, Figma, Framer and Apple event pages.** Steal: editorial restraint, a monochrome plus single-accent rule, stark high contrast, full-bleed sections and type as image. All converge on one typeface family, a restrained palette plus one accent, high contrast and motion with a defined curve set.

---

## Anti-patterns

- Framework-heavy scaffolds for what is fundamentally a static document. Vanilla HTML plus minimal JS is right.
- Pulling in a presentation library you do not control for what is 40 lines of JS. Steal the patterns instead.
- Multiple ideas on one slide because there is space. Split it.
- Icons or illustrations that decorate without clarifying. Delete them.
- Reusing a slide's pattern immediately after itself. Vary the rhythm.
- Symmetric enter and exit motion.
- Contrast collapse over a background image.
- Animating font metrics. Use transform scale for visual size.
- A missing reduced-motion block.
- Reflow inside the stage: clamp, vw or vh used inside a fixed canvas.
- A single stage that only scales down. It is unreadable on a phone.
- A page background that differs from the slides.
- Text under 20 pixels authored on a landscape canvas.
- Embedded fonts or font-face rules.
- Any CDN font, stylesheet or script.
- Portrait with two columns, tiny chart labels or hover-only controls.

# Presentation narrative craft

Working reference for narrative and communication decisions. Load at the narrative critique pass to check the throughline and pick a frame; load again at the outline step to structure the beats.

## The two-axis picker (the whole toolkit in one table)

Density and narrative are orthogonal picks, not a single dial. Density is the platform decision: how much information sits on the slide. Narrative posture is the rhetorical decision: whether the audience derives the answer from an arc or receives it up front. A throughline (one idea the whole deck ladders to) runs against every cell as a cutting rule. If a slide does not serve the throughline, cut it.

|  | Answer-forward (state, then evidence) | Narrative-forward (arc, then land) |
|---|---|---|
| **Low density** (speaker carries meaning aloud) | Minto and SCQA spoken; Before-After-Bridge as a compact opener. Sparse assertion slides with spoken evidence. Fit: live executive updates, town halls. | Sparkline plus a memorable moment; story spine; five-act arc. Fit: talks, webinars, customer case-study segments. |
| **High density** (reader carries meaning off the page) | Minto Pyramid SCQA (answer first, then proof pillars); the ten-slide venture sequence; the 10/20/30 rule; Before-After-Bridge as compact framing. Fit: pitch deck, proposal, executive-read decks. | Strategic narrative in five parts (plus a name-the-enemy opener for incumbent-disruption pitches); the six-page memo; the working-backwards press release and FAQ; narrative distillation; sparkline at density; spine at density. Fit: investor memos, founder essays, decision-forcing internal docs, read-through sales decks. |

**How to pick.** Density first, keyed off delivery mode and audience posture. Narrative second, keyed off whether the audience will accept the answer before the arc has been earned. When the brief is silent on posture, default to the diagonal: low density goes narrative-forward; high density goes answer-forward. Only leave the diagonal when a named reason is on the brief.

## Narrative frameworks (pick-list)

Each entry: owner, one-line description, when to reach for it, and skeleton.

- **Freytag's five-act arc** (Freytag). Exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, denouement. Reach for it on a story about work already done: a case study, retrospective or war story. Weak fit for advocacy, because presentations often need many climaxes.
- **Sparkline / what is versus what could be** (Duarte). Oscillate between the audience's current reality and the future you are pitching; build to a new-baseline ending. Every talk should have a big idea in one full sentence and at least one memorable moment: a dramatization, an evocative visual, an emotive story, a shocking statistic or a repeatable sound bite. Reach for it on talks and webinars.
- **Story spine** (Kenn Adams). Eight beats: once upon a time, every day, until one day, because of that, because of that, because of that, until finally, and ever since then. Each because-of-that beat must be causal, not chronological. Reach for it for a founding story or a user story that needs to earn its emotional beats.
- **SCQA and the Minto Pyramid** (Barbara Minto). Situation, complication, question, answer, supported by a mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive pyramid. Answer first, evidence below. Reach for it whenever the audience is an executive, investor or buyer who reads to decide.
- **Before-After-Bridge** (direct-response canon). Before (current pain), after (world once solved), bridge (your offer). Compact and hope-forward. Weakness: easy to overpromise or shame the before.
- **The ten-slide venture sequence** (Sequoia Capital). Purpose, problem, solution, why now, market size, competition, product, business model, team, financials. Why now is the load-bearing slide. Reach for it as the default pitch-deck skeleton unless you have a named reason to deviate.
- **The 10/20/30 rule** (Guy Kawasaki). Ten slides, twenty minutes, no font under 30 point. The same ten-slide bound with font and time discipline attached.
- **The throughline** (Chris Anderson). Not a sequence, a cutting rule. One major idea; everything ladders back to it. Reach for it whenever an outline feels like two talks glued together.
- **Strategic narrative in five parts** (Andy Raskin). Name a big relevant change in the world; show winners and losers; tease the promised land; introduce features as gifts for overcoming obstacles; present evidence you can make the story come true. Reach for it on read-through sales and investor artifacts where the audience must feel the stakes before the product.
- **Name the enemy** (Andy Raskin). When stakes come from a legible antagonist, replace the first beat with the named enemy. Reach for it on incumbent-disruption pitches where the villain is a specific product or behaviour the audience already resents.
- **The six-page narrative memo** (Amazon). Six pages maximum, single-spaced, a silent read at the start of a meeting, then discussion. Reach for it for internal decision-forcing docs, business reviews and board updates. Density is the argument; slide polish would let a bad idea past.
- **The working-backwards press release and FAQ** (Amazon). A one-page mock press release plus a short FAQ, written as if the product had already launched, then work backwards to the spec. Reach for it for new-product proposals where the team needs a forcing function to define the customer outcome first.
- **Narrative distillation** (Kevin Kwok). Founder-authored narrative as compounding leverage; the chief executive's job is to distill the multi-year thesis for investors, employees and customers at once. Reach for it for founder-authored investor memos, IPO framing and long-form strategy essays.

## Visual storytelling and minimal-text principles

What makes a low-density deck work:

- **Maximum effect with minimum means; naturalness; understated elegance; negative space as an element.** You earn a full-bleed image slide by having removed everything else on that slide. A blank or black slide is a beat, not a bug.
- **One idea per slide plus assertion headlines.** Replace the topic-phrase headline with a sentence that states the slide's actual claim, and support it with visual evidence, not a bulleted list. On high-density decks, every slide's headline should be a claim someone could disagree with, not a topic label.
- **Exactly one memorable moment per low-density deck:** a moment engineered to be repeated later.
- **Chart density and small multiples** (Tufte). Maximize data-ink ratio; kill chartjunk; prefer small multiples over stacked series. A chart with five series and no annotation is almost always worse than five small multiples with the point annotated in the space a legend would waste.
- **Rule of three, a planted sound bite, modelled emotion and rehearsed recovery.** Put the tagline in press materials, then repeat it on stage as promise, demonstration and confirmed fact.
- **Pair narration with a diagram, not with the same words on screen.**
- **Honest counter-note.** Minimal slides raise the cost of a bad delivery; they do not lower it. A nearly blank slide only works if the speaker carries all the meaning aloud.

## Communication anti-patterns

- **Wall-of-text slideument.** Split into 3 to 5 slides, one claim each; move prose to speaker notes.
- **Bullet bloat with a phrase headline.** Use a sentence-assertion headline and one visual.
- **Reading the slide aloud.** If the words on the slide are the script, you have a document, not a deck.
- **A chart with five series and no annotation.** Use small multiples with the point annotated on the mark.
- **Two talks glued together.** Apply the throughline test; cut everything that does not ladder to it.
- **Overpromising in the after of a before-after-bridge.** Ground the after in what is actually true.
- **A sparkline without a memorable moment.**
- **Answer-first for an audience that does not yet believe the shift.** Front-load the change and the winners and losers before the answer.
- **Narrative-forward for an executive who reads to decide.** Put the answer on the first slide; the arc can carry the appendix.

## Escalation

If the brief is silent on posture, or the audience posture and the density call point at different cells, flag it in the narrative critique comment. Do not guess. Push back on a broken brief before you dress it up.

# Visual design patterns

Reference library for on-brand raster deliverables: social posts, event covers, thumbnails, webinar cards, open-graph images and hero art. Use this as a menu: not every piece uses every pattern, and no piece should use them all. One idea per composition still rules.

The first half is the pattern library. The second half is the tactical craft that separates an AI-generic composition from world-class on-brand craft.

## The rendering pipeline (how the piece gets made)

Every deliverable is authored as a single-file HTML page at the target dimensions, then rendered to raster by opening it on your own computer at that size and taking a screenshot. You do not hand-write SVG in isolation and hope it rasterizes; that path hides broken fonts, contrast collapses and text overflow. Rendered pixels are the evidence.

1. **Author an HTML file** at the exact target dimensions (for example 1080 by 1350 portrait, 1200 by 628 landscape, 1280 by 720, 1920 by 1080). Inline all CSS. Use the brand typeface if it is available locally; otherwise say in your message that the render uses the system font.
2. **Open the file on your own computer** at the target size and wait until fonts have loaded.
3. **Take a screenshot.** That PNG is your raster deliverable. Render at double scale if a retina master is asked for.
4. **Also extract a scalable SVG master** for pieces that are pure geometry and type.
5. **Save the raster, and the SVG master if applicable,** and attach it to the job object. The HTML source is authoring scaffolding, not a deliverable unless the requester asks for it.

**Why HTML over SVG only:** real variable fonts, kerning and proper text wrapping only render correctly when a real browser lays them out. Screenshots let you see what you produced instead of writing SVG blind.

## Fixed-canvas rules (non-negotiable)

- **Author every element in pixels against the target canvas.** No vw, vh or clamp inside the piece.
- **Safe margins:** 64 pixels outer padding for portrait and landscape social; 96 pixels for event covers and thumbnails. Full-bleed geometry ignores it; text never touches the edge.
- **One composition per file.** A carousel is one file per frame, rendered separately.
- **Baseline grid:** pick a rhythm (8 pixels is standard) and snap positions and line-heights to it. Break the grid deliberately, once, if the piece calls for a memorable moment.

## Target dimensions (starting list)

Match the requested format; ask if genuinely ambiguous.

- **Portrait social post:** 1080 by 1350
- **Landscape social post and open-graph image:** 1200 by 628
- **Video thumbnail:** 1280 by 720
- **Event cover and webinar card:** 1920 by 1080 (or 1200 by 630 if the platform constrains it)
- **Square social post:** 1080 by 1080
- **Hero and landing-page header:** brief-driven, but hold a fixed aspect ratio

## Type scale (starting point, adjust to brand tokens)

- **Event covers and video thumbnails:** hero phrase 120 to 200 pixels, small mark 32 to 48.
- **Portrait social:** hero phrase 96 to 140, small mark 28 to 36.
- **Landscape social and open-graph:** hero phrase 72 to 108, small mark 24 to 32.
- **Webinar cards:** trend more editorial and restrained: hero phrase 64 to 96, generous whitespace, longer subheads permitted.

Match scale to the feeling register you picked. Thumbnails and event covers earn bigger, more confident scale; webinar cards trend editorial.

## Composition patterns (the library)

Each pattern is a compositional template. Pick one per piece, do not stack them. Names are the vocabulary; use them when proposing the three-style probe.

- **Hero and headline:** full-bleed abstract background (SVG geometry or a graded photo), single hero phrase over it, optional small mark.
- **Statement:** one sentence, oversized, centred on generous whitespace. Rare; works when the copy alone is the whole idea.
- **Editorial column:** headline stacked over a photo or geometric mark; caption or subhead beneath in a smaller weight.
- **Data callout:** one big number (half the canvas height), one-line caption underneath, optional source citation. If you have three numbers, use three-column instead.
- **Three-column:** three parallel items, equal weight, identical structure per column. Never four.
- **Quote pull:** pull quote in editorial hierarchy, attribution in caption size. Never more than 25 words.
- **Comparison:** two-column before and after, us and them, then and now. Label the axis in a small caption above.
- **Image and caption:** full-bleed or half-bleed photo graded to the brand palette, caption in a corner.
- **Diagram:** inline SVG for arrows, nodes and flow. Rare on social; common on hero art.
- **Abstract geometry field:** no text, pure brand-native geometry. Use for untitled hero art where the requester will lay copy on top in a downstream layout.

## Feeling register (name it before you compose)

Pick 1 or 2 from this vocabulary: dramatic, techy, playful, professional, calm, editorial. Save the choice on the job object. Every composition choice traces back to it.

- **Palette temperature and contrast:** dramatic and techy run high-contrast; calm and professional run low-contrast; playful runs unexpected pairings.
- **Type scale:** dramatic and playful live at the top of the scale; professional and editorial at the bottom.
- **Geometry style:** techy runs a precise grid and a monochrome accent; playful runs a looser layout and a broader palette; editorial runs magazine hierarchy and quote pulls.

If a register was not specified, ask. If the person cannot answer, pick one and name it explicitly. Never leave the register implicit.

## The three-style probe (mandatory before committing)

Before you commit to a single direction, propose three style variations, called safe, bold and wildcard, as one representative composition each. This is a cheaper redirect point than a finished piece.

- **Safe:** closest to the established visual language, minimum risk, always shippable.
- **Bold:** pushes one axis (scale, palette contrast, composition asymmetry). The strongest version you can argue for.
- **Wildcard:** deliberately off-register. Different palette, different geometry, different mood. Often rejected, but occasionally unlocks something the brief missed.

Render each probe through the full pipeline and attach the three PNGs to the job object in one message. Ask which to develop. Do not ship all three as final options; ship one direction, chosen.

## Backgrounds

- **Author SVG geometry** for anything abstract: brand-native shapes, brand palette, sharp edges over gradient blobs.
- **Photos** only when the subject matters. Grade to the brand palette so they do not feel foreign. Full-bleed photos with text overlaid must pass the contrast rules below.
- **Banned:** gradient mesh blobs, grey noise fills, generic 3D shapes, generic particle grids, filler droplets, glowing neon fields, plastic 3D blobs, glossy purple sheen, wireframe globes.

---

## Craft depth (world-class layer)

The patterns above cover the what. This section covers the how well: the craft that separates production-grade visuals from templates.

### Typography

- **One family used systemically.** Never fall back to a system sans as a hero typeface; use the brand family or say plainly that it is unavailable.
- **Variable fonts, weight as a range.** Compose weight as a design decision, not a picked value.
- **Turn on font-optical-sizing: auto** at the root so optical sizing tracks computed size. At display sizes this gives the type designer's actual display cut.
- **Kerning at display sizes matters more than at body sizes.**
- **Wait for fonts to be ready** before the screenshot. A screenshot taken during a font swap captures the fallback rendering.

### Fixed-canvas rendering (spelled out)

- Author every element in pixels against the exact target canvas.
- Set the HTML body to exactly the target width and height.
- Set the browser viewport to exactly the target dimensions.
- Take the screenshot clipped to the target size. This locks the output pixel-perfect.
- For retina delivery, render again at double scale: same viewport, double pixel output.
- **Never use clamp, vw or vh inside the composition.**

### Motion: a curve library, not one curve

For static raster deliverables motion does not apply directly, but if a variant needs to repeat, use the same discipline.

- cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1) for professional registers.
- cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1) for calm and editorial registers.
- cubic-bezier(0.5, 1.15, 0.4, 1) for playful registers only.
- **Never linear.**

Entrances ease out over 250 to 400 ms; exits ease in over 150 to 250 ms. Never symmetric. Always ship a reduced-motion block for any motion variant.

### Full-bleed images: contrast discipline

Text needs 4.5 to 1 contrast against its background (3 to 1 for large text). Over an image, the ratio must hold at the lightest and darkest pixels behind each glyph.

- **Scrim:** a dark overlay or a gradient biased toward the text edge.
- **Duotone:** an SVG colour matrix or a CSS filter chain to lock the palette to brand hues.
- **Compose the photo for the type:** place hero phrases in the darkest quadrant deliberately.
- **Text shadow is a last resort.**

### SVG craft: generative geometry that reads brand-native

Inline SVG so you can animate paths, use masks and clip paths, and drive fills from CSS variables.

- **Voronoi cells:** cellular, organic-technical.
- **Phyllotaxis point clouds:** Fibonacci spiral, sunflower-seed packing.
- **Noise fields:** turbulence and displacement for organic textures, behind text only when the contrast rules hold.
- **Flow lines** from a parametric field: directional without arrows.
- **Concentric geometry:** nested circles, sequenced arcs, radial grids.

Rules: keep any single background SVG under 20 KB inline; strip editor metadata before inlining; drive fills from CSS variables.

### Colour and palette discipline

- **2 or 3 hues per piece.** Not four. If you reach for a fourth, one of the first three is doing too much work.
- **Brand primary plus one accent plus one neutral** is the default.
- **Pair tones for hierarchy:** hero text in the highest-contrast pair, small marks in a mid-contrast pair. Never both at the same contrast.
- **Test the palette at full zoom and at thumbnail size.** If the thumbnail is muddy, the palette is wrong.

### Rendering QA checklist (every piece before ship)

After the screenshot lands, run this against the PNG, not the HTML:

- **Contrast:** hero phrase and any body text legible against whatever sits behind it.
- **Containment:** all content sits inside the target canvas, nothing clipped or bleeding.
- **Completeness:** no missing visual, no broken image, no unloaded font fallback.
- **Layout:** matches the composition pattern intent; no collapsed columns, no overlap hiding text.
- **On-brand tokens:** colours match the brand hex codes; type is the brand family or the fallback was stated.
- **Register match:** squint at the piece. A calm piece that reads dramatic is off-brief.

If any check fails, fix the HTML, render and screenshot again. Do not ship a piece with a known bug.

### Reference stacks: what to steal, what to leave

- **Stripe:** editorial restraint, generous whitespace, a measured accent. Leave the bespoke illustration style.
- **Linear:** monochrome plus a single-accent rule, a strict grid behind everything. Leave the specific palette.
- **Vercel:** stark black and white, a large hero rule, full-bleed sections. Leave the dark-by-default aesthetic if the brand is light.
- **Apple event pages:** full-bleed, type as image, one message per view.
- **Pentagram covers:** editorial typographic composition, unexpected type scale, deliberate asymmetry.
- **IBM and Braun:** restraint and functional beauty, one typeface family, a restrained palette plus one accent.

All converge on: one typeface family, a restrained palette plus one accent, high contrast, and composition that earns its space.

---

## Anti-patterns

- **System-default display type** as the hero typeface. Ship the brand family or say it is unavailable.
- **Gradient blobs, grey noise fills, generic particle grids, meaningless droplets, plastic 3D blobs, glowing neon fields, wireframe globes, glossy purple sheen.** Ban them from every piece.
- **Symmetric enter and exit motion.**
- **Contrast collapse over a background image.**
- **Multiple ideas on one composition** because there is space.
- **Icons or marks that decorate without meaning.**
- **Four columns, four hues or four ideas.** Three is the natural limit.
- **Reusing a pattern across a series without variation.** Vary the pattern while holding the palette and type family.
- **A missing reduced-motion block** on motion variants.
- **Shipping without the render step.** If your computer cannot open the file, say so on the job object and stop. Do not fall back to saying the source looks fine.

31b5ba88-57ef-404e-bd9a-32b02d646015.name: viewer-safe-html
31b5ba88-57ef-404e-bd9a-32b02d646015.description: How to publish an HTML prototype, mock-up, deck or mini-app so it renders correctly in the built-in file viewer. The viewer runs HTML in a locked-down frame that blocks every outside script, stylesheet, font and image, and blocks local storage, so pages built with a CSS framework CDN, web fonts or an icon CDN look unstyled and half empty there while looking fine on a laptop. Load before you create or update any HTML file, and run the check script before you upload.
31b5ba88-57ef-404e-bd9a-32b02d646015.content:
---
name: viewer-safe-html
description: How to publish an HTML prototype, mock-up, deck or mini-app so it renders correctly in the built-in file viewer. The viewer runs HTML in a locked-down frame that blocks every outside script, stylesheet, font and image, and blocks local storage, so pages built with a CSS framework CDN, web fonts or an icon CDN look unstyled and half empty there while looking fine on a laptop. Load before you create or update any HTML file, and run the check script before you upload.
---

# Viewer-safe HTML

The viewer shows HTML inside a sandboxed frame with a strict content policy that the page cannot relax. Pages that depend on outside resources look perfect locally and show up unstyled with empty panels in the viewer.

## Why it breaks

The frame allows inline styles and inline scripts and blocks everything from the network:

- Inline style blocks and inline scripts work.
- Any script, stylesheet or font from the internet is blocked.
- Font files are blocked, even as data URLs. Use a system font stack. Never embed a font: a base64 font adds about 130 KB per face and shows nothing.
- Images only work as data URLs or inline SVG.
- Fetch, XHR, forms and websockets are blocked.
- Local storage and session storage throw a security error. One uncaught throw stops the whole script tag, so everything built after it, tabs and panels, never appears.

## Rules

1. One self-contained file. No src or href pointing at http or https.
2. Use a utility CSS framework only through a build step that compiles it into a normal style block. Do not ship the browser CDN.
3. Icons: inline the SVG. Do not rely on an icon script from a CDN.
4. Fonts: use the system font stack and nothing else. No font-face, no data font, no font file of any kind.
5. Storage: leave local storage and session storage calls as they are. The build script adds a small in-memory fallback when access throws, so page code is never rewritten. Values do not persist between visits in the viewer.
6. Keep the editable source with CDN tags for local preview. Upload only the built output.
7. After the build, the script prints viewer-safe OK, a WARN line or a FAIL line. Do not upload on WARN or FAIL. FAIL means a font-face rule, a data font URI, or, for a deck, a file over 150 KB. A WARN says the built CSS has no theme variables or lost some the page declared: the theme block was missed, so look at the style tags in the source.

## Build and publish

One-time in your sandbox: create a folder, install the CSS and icon packages you need, and save the script below as viewer-safe.mjs. Copy your source HTML there, then run it with the source and output paths. For a deck add the deck flag: a deck must be under 150 KB.

Upload the built file through the workspace file API from the shell, not by retyping long content into a create call; long content gets cut off silently (see the upload-binary-file skill). The sandbox exposes the workspace API as three environment variables: one ending in API_URL (the base URL), one ending in API_KEY, and one ending in WORKSPACE_ID. Read them from the environment.

Check before you say done: open the built HTML in a browser with storage blocked and confirm the tabs or main panels are present. Say what you checked.

## viewer-safe.mjs

```js
// usage: node viewer-safe.mjs in.html out.html   (run inside a dir where the CSS and icon packages were installed)
import fs from 'fs'
import { execSync } from 'child_process'
const [inp, outp] = process.argv.slice(2).filter((a) => !a.startsWith('--'))
const deck = process.argv.includes('--deck')
let html = fs.readFileSync(inp, 'utf8')
const styleRe = /<style type="text\/tailwindcss">([\s\S]*?)<\/style>/
// match on a copy with comment text blanked out, so a header comment that quotes the style tag is never picked
const masked = html.replace(/<!--[\s\S]*?-->/g, (c) => ' '.repeat(c.length))
const m = styleRe.exec(masked)
let declared = []
if (m) {
  let css = html.slice(m.index, m.index + m[0].length).match(styleRe)[1]
  declared = [...new Set(css.replace(/@theme[^{]*\{[^}]*\}/g, '').match(/--[\w-]+(?=\s*:)/g) ?? [])]
  css = css.replace(/--font-sans:[^;]*;/, '--font-sans: ui-sans-serif, system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, Arial, sans-serif;')
  css = css.replace(/--font-mono:[^;]*;/, '--font-mono: ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Consolas, monospace;')
  fs.writeFileSync('.vs-in.css', `@import "tailwindcss";\n@source "${process.cwd()}/${inp}";\n` + css)
  execSync('npx @tailwindcss/cli -i .vs-in.css -o .vs-out.css --minify', { stdio: 'inherit' })
  html = html.slice(0, m.index) + '<style>' + fs.readFileSync('.vs-out.css', 'utf8') + '</style>' + html.slice(m.index + m[0].length)
}
html = html.replace(/\s*<link[^>]*(preconnect|fonts\.googleapis)[^>]*>/g, '')
html = html.replace(/\s*<script[^>]*\ssrc="https?:[^"]*"[^>]*><\/script>/g, '')
const svg = (n, c) => {
  const s = fs.readFileSync(`node_modules/lucide-static/icons/${n}.svg`, 'utf8').replace(/<!--[\s\S]*?-->/, '')
  const inner = s.match(/<svg[^>]*>([\s\S]*)<\/svg>/)[1].replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim()
  return `<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true" class="${c}">${inner}</svg>`
}
html = html.replace(/<i data-lucide=\\?"([\w-]+)\\?" class=\\?"([^"\\]*)\\?"><\/i>/g, (_, n, c) => svg(n, c))
const shim = `<script>(function(){try{window.localStorage.length;window.sessionStorage.length;return}catch(e){}var mk=function(){var d={};return{getItem:function(k){return Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(d,k)?d[k]:null},setItem:function(k,v){d[k]=String(v)},removeItem:function(k){delete d[k]},clear:function(){d={}},key:function(i){return Object.keys(d)[i]||null},get length(){return Object.keys(d).length}}};['localStorage','sessionStorage'].forEach(function(n){try{Object.defineProperty(window,n,{configurable:true,value:mk()})}catch(e){}})})()</script>`
html = /<head[^>]*>/i.test(html) ? html.replace(/<head[^>]*>/i, (h) => h + shim) : shim + html
fs.writeFileSync(outp, html)
const bad = html.match(/https?:\/\/(?!www\.w3\.org)[^\s"'<>)]*/g)?.filter((u) => /\.(js|css|woff2?)\b|fonts\.|cdn|unpkg/.test(u)) ?? []
const css = [...html.matchAll(/<style[^>]*>([\s\S]*?)<\/style>/g)].map((x) => x[1]).join('\n')
const noTheme = !/(^|[;{}\s])--(?!tw-)[\w-]+\s*:/.test(css)
const lost = declared.filter((v) => !css.includes(v + ':'))
const left = [noTheme && 'built CSS has no theme variables (--name: value); the theme style block was probably missed, so the page may be unstyled', lost.length && 'theme variables missing from built CSS: ' + lost.join(', '), /data-lucide/.test(html) && 'data-lucide left (JS-built icon? inline the svg)', bad.length && 'external refs: ' + bad.join(', ')].filter(Boolean)
const fatal = [/@font-face/.test(html) && '@font-face found (fonts are blocked in the viewer, use the system font stack)', /data:(font|application\/(x-)?font)/.test(html) && 'data:font URI found (remove it)', deck && Buffer.byteLength(html) > 150 * 1024 && 'deck is ' + Math.round(Buffer.byteLength(html) / 1024) + ' KB, the limit is 150 KB'].filter(Boolean)
if (fatal.length) { console.log('FAIL: ' + fatal.join('; '), outp); process.exit(1) }
console.log(left.length ? 'WARN: ' + left.join('; ') : 'viewer-safe OK', outp)
```

2520d820-a06f-46c1-9203-8c970bea7ffe.name: frontend-design
2520d820-a06f-46c1-9203-8c970bea7ffe.description: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that do not read as templated defaults.
2520d820-a06f-46c1-9203-8c970bea7ffe.content:
---
name: frontend-design
description: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that do not read as templated defaults.
---

# Frontend design

Approach this as the design lead at a studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. The client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if it is justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the person. You can propose one concrete subject, the design's audience and its primary job. The subject's industry, materials and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from. A design for a toy for 8 to 11 year olds will be very different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content throughout.

## Design principles

The hero is the first thing viewers see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that fits best: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment. A big number with a small label, supporting stats and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that is truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You do not need a different typeface for display and body; use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct. Choose typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths and spacing. When type is a headline or visual element, use the treatment itself as part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle.

Default to line lengths under 80 characters. Serif typefaces can take slightly longer lines; give serif body text a little more line-height than sans.

Avoid these default typographic treatments, the commonest tells of a generated page:

- Accenting a single word or phrase in a headline with italic, bold or a different colour.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers and labels should encode useful information rather than decorate. Numbered markers are only appropriate when the content really is a sequence. Check before adding them.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. One orchestrated moment lands better than scattered effects. Fade-and-slide entrances on every section and hover transitions on every card read as generated. Motion that answers a person's action is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a brief has no real copy and it is up to you to write placeholder copy. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

AI-generated design clusters around a few traits:

1. A warm cream background with a high-contrast serif display and a warm-clay accent.
2. A near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent.
3. A broadsheet layout with hairline rules, zero border radius and dense newspaper columns.
4. The software-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow under each, gradient washes as decoration.
5. Template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out all-caps eyebrow above every heading, meta strings joined with middle dots, labels built as word, dash, fragment, tinted near-black standing in for black, a monospace face for small data labels, an arrow appended to every link and button.

All are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a direction, follow it exactly. Where it leaves an axis free, do not spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan from the brief: a compact token system with colour, type, layout and principles.

- Colour: describe the core base palette as 4 to 6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept with one-sentence prose and rough wireframes to compare; include alignment guidance.
- Principles: what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building. If any part reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise it and say what changed and why. Only after you have confirmed the plan's relative uniqueness should you write code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful with CSS selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, especially with a type-based selector and an element-based selector. This often shows up in padding and margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it. Before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copy that you bring to spacing and colour. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook configuration. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users beats being clever.

Use active voice by default. A call to action says exactly what happens when it is used: Save changes, not Submit. An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says Publish produces a message that says Published. The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors do not apologize and are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

27b7b7f3-3274-4b49-afa1-81ab68340396.name: upload-binary-file
27b7b7f3-3274-4b49-afa1-81ab68340396.description: How to save a binary file (spreadsheet, document, presentation, PDF, image, archive) from your sandbox into workspace files without retyping base64 in a tool call. Load whenever you need to create or replace a file that is not plain text, or any file over about 15,000 characters of base64. Retyping base64 inside a create or update call gets cut off silently above roughly 20,000 characters and can overwrite a good file with a broken one. Use curl from the shell instead.
27b7b7f3-3274-4b49-afa1-81ab68340396.content:
---
name: upload-binary-file
description: How to save a binary file (spreadsheet, document, presentation, PDF, image, archive) from your sandbox into workspace files without retyping base64 in a tool call. Load whenever you need to create or replace a file that is not plain text, or any file over about 15,000 characters of base64. Retyping base64 inside a create or update call gets cut off silently above roughly 20,000 characters and can overwrite a good file with a broken one. Use curl from the shell instead.
---

# Upload a binary file from the sandbox

## The rule

Never paste base64 into a create or update call for a binary file bigger than about 10 KB. The model cuts off the base64 it retypes, and the server stores whatever it gets. A real case: an 80 KB image was overwritten by a 1,792 byte file and the call said success.

Instead, let a program move the bytes. Your sandbox has curl, jq, base64, sha256sum and stat.

## Step 0: check the environment

The sandbox exposes the workspace API as three environment variables: one ending in API_URL (the base URL), one ending in API_KEY, and one ending in WORKSPACE_ID. Read their names from the environment and export them under short names:

    API_URL="${<prefix>_API_URL}"
    API_KEY="${<prefix>_API_KEY}"
    WORKSPACE_ID="${<prefix>_WORKSPACE_ID}"
    for v in API_URL API_KEY WORKSPACE_ID; do test -n "${!v}" || { echo "missing $v, stop and tell the person"; exit 1; }; done

If a variable is missing, stop. Do not fall back to retyping base64.

## Step 1: create a new file

Set F to the path of your file and MIME to its type (spreadsheets use application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet, documents use application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document, presentations use application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.presentationml.presentation, PDF is application/pdf, PNG is image/png).

    F=/path/to/budget.xlsx
    MIME=application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet
    B64=$(mktemp); BODY=$(mktemp); RESP=$(mktemp)
    base64 -w0 "$F" > "$B64"
    jq -n --arg name "$(basename "$F")" --arg mime "$MIME" --rawfile content "$B64" \
      --argjson size "$(stat -c %s "$F")" --arg sha "$(sha256sum "$F" | cut -d' ' -f1)" \
      '{name:$name, mime_type:$mime, encoding:"base64", content:$content, expected_size_bytes:$size, expected_sha256:$sha}' > "$BODY"
    curl -sS -o "$RESP" -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST "$API_URL/api/files" \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" -H "X-Workspace-Id: $WORKSPACE_ID" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" --data-binary @"$BODY"

Rules that matter:

- base64 -w0 (no line wrapping). Wrapped base64 is rejected.
- Build the JSON with jq --rawfile and send with curl --data-binary @file. Never pass the content with jq --arg or on the command line; the argument limit is about 128 KB.
- expected_size_bytes and expected_sha256 are harmless today and become enforced checks when the guard ships. Always send them.
- There is no small size cap; very large uploads are untested. If an upload is refused, record the file size and the error, and report it. Do not split the file by hand.

## Step 2: replace an existing file

Same body without name and mime_type, sent as PATCH to /api/files/FILE_ID.

    jq -n --rawfile content "$B64" --argjson size "$(stat -c %s "$F")" --arg sha "$(sha256sum "$F" | cut -d' ' -f1)" \
      '{encoding:"base64", content:$content, expected_size_bytes:$size, expected_sha256:$sha}' > "$BODY"
    curl -sS -o "$RESP" -w "%{http_code}\n" -X PATCH "$API_URL/api/files/FILE_ID" \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" -H "X-Workspace-Id: $WORKSPACE_ID" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" --data-binary @"$BODY"

Always send encoding base64 on a binary replace. Without it the server stores the base64 text itself as the file and still says success.

Before replacing, read the old size with a GET on the file. If your new file is less than half the old size, stop and ask the person, because you are probably about to destroy a good file. Only overwrite when the shrink is intended.

## Step 3: verify, every time

The response must be HTTP 201 for create or 200 for replace, and sizeBytes must equal the local size.

    test "$(jq -r .sizeBytes "$RESP")" = "$(stat -c %s "$F")" || echo "SIZE MISMATCH, do not report success"

For a stronger check, read it back and compare the hash:

    curl -sS "$API_URL/api/files/FILE_ID" -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" -H "X-Workspace-Id: $WORKSPACE_ID" \
      | jq -r .content | base64 -d | sha256sum
    sha256sum "$F"

The two hashes must match. If anything differs, say so in your report. Never tell the person the file is uploaded when the check failed.

## Step 4: attach and share

The response has a url field. Link it in your message. To attach it to an object, create a relationship with the object as source, the file id as target, and type attached. Clean up: rm -f "$B64" "$BODY" "$RESP".

## What to tell the person

Say the file name, size, that the hash matched, and the url. For customer documents, also say a person should open the downloaded file in the original app before it goes anywhere external; some viewers offer download only.

## If it fails

- 400 with invalid base64: you used wrapped base64 or edited the string. Redo with base64 -w0 from the original file.
- 413 or a proxy error on a large file: report the size and the status code to the person. Do not split the file by hand.
- 401 or 403: the key or workspace id is wrong. Stop and tell the person.
- Environment variables missing or curl not found: stop and report it.

---
name: coding-discipline
description: The four principles every agent producing an artifact (code, prototype, deck or HTML page) applies before shipping. Adapted from Andrej Karpathy's LLM coding guidelines. Activate whenever you are about to write, edit or approve any produced artifact.
---

# Coding discipline

Four principles. Every agent producing an artifact (code, prototype, deck or HTML page) applies all four before shipping. They exist because artifacts that skip these steps waste reviewer time and erode the person's willingness to review at all.

## 1. Think before coding

Do not assume. Do not hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.

Before you build:

- State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask one specific question on the object.
- If multiple interpretations exist, name them. Do not silently pick one.
- If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.
- If something is unclear, stop. Name what is confusing. Ask. Do not paper over ambiguity with a guess.

## 2. Simplicity first

Minimum artifact that satisfies the spec. Nothing speculative.

- No features beyond what was asked.
- No abstractions for single-use code.
- No flexibility or configurability that was not requested.
- No error handling for impossible scenarios.
- If you wrote 200 lines, 20 slides or 5 sections and it could be a quarter of that, rewrite it.

Ask: would a senior person in this discipline call this overcomplicated? If yes, cut.

## 3. Surgical changes

Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.

When editing existing work:

- Do not improve adjacent code, copy, layout or formatting.
- Do not refactor things that are not broken.
- Match the existing style, even if you would do it differently.
- If you notice unrelated dead code, stale copy or a broken component, flag it. Do not fix it in this change.

When your change creates orphans:

- Remove imports, variables, functions, slides and sections that your change made unused.
- Do not remove pre-existing dead content unless asked.

The test: every changed line traces directly to the acceptance criteria or spec.

## 4. Goal-driven execution

Define success criteria. Iterate until verified.

Turn vague briefs into verifiable goals:

- Add validation becomes: write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass.
- Fix the bug becomes: write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass.
- Design the inbox becomes: the prototype covers every state at every breakpoint; screenshots attached.
- Build the deck becomes: every slide passes the visual check; a screenshot grid is attached.

For multi-step work, state a brief plan up front, one line per step and how you will verify it. Strong success criteria let you iterate autonomously. Weak criteria force constant clarification.

---

**These principles are working if:** fewer unnecessary changes in diffs, fewer rewrites from over-engineering, and clarifying questions arrive before mistakes, not after.
